title: Which of these numbers is a product of exactly three different primes?
description: Each of the five numbers is split into primes by dividing with primes from the list, and the primes are counted. Only one number splits into three different primes with none repeated.
teaching_notes: One idea: split a number into primes and look at the primes that come out, because a repeated prime or a fourth prime rules the number out. Watch for students who pick sixty because it has three different primes inside it.

video_script.why: The child divides each number by primes from the sieve list until only primes are left, and then counts the different primes.
video_script.substitution: Divide each number by the smallest prime that fits and keep going until only primes remain.
video_script.anchor: Five number cards, each split into primes by dividing with primes from the list
video_script.payoff_line: One hundred and five is the product of exactly three different primes, three times five times seven.

final_answer.spoken: one hundred and five is the one

video_script.design: Each number card is split into prime cards; a card that repeats a prime or has a fourth prime turns amber and the card with three different primes turns teal.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; five number cards 45, 60, 91, 105, 330; the words exactly three different primes

marks.cards: the five number cards appear in a row
marks.ask: the words exactly three different primes light up

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about products of primes.
<bookmark mark='cards'/>Five numbers are given, forty five, sixty, ninety one, one hundred and five, and three hundred and thirty.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which of them is the product of exactly three different primes?

beats.on_screen: the five cards stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: split a number by dividing with primes from the list until only primes are left; different = no prime repeats

marks.split: a number card splits into prime cards
marks.diff: a repeated prime is shown with a warning tick

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>We split a number by dividing it with primes from the list, until only primes are left.
<bookmark mark='diff'/>Three different primes means that no prime repeats.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the five numbers on the cards.

beats.on_screen: To find: the product of exactly three different primes

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the number that is exactly three different primes multiplied.

marks.forty: forty five splits into three, three and five and turns amber
marks.ninety: ninety one splits into seven and thirteen and turns amber

narration: <bookmark mark='forty'/>Step one, split the first two numbers. Forty five is three times three times five, so three repeats.
<bookmark mark='ninety'/>Ninety one is seven times thirteen, which is only two primes. Both numbers are ruled out.

marks.sixty: sixty splits into two, two, three and five and turns amber
marks.three: three hundred and thirty splits into four different primes and turns amber

narration: <bookmark mark='sixty'/>Step two, split sixty. It is two times two times three times five, so two repeats.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Three hundred and thirty is two times three times five times eleven, which is four different primes. Both numbers are ruled out.

marks.divide: one hundred and five is divided by three to give thirty five
marks.split: thirty five splits into five and seven and the three primes turn teal

narration: <bookmark mark='divide'/>Step three, split one hundred and five. Three divides it, and the answer is thirty five.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Thirty five is five times seven, so the primes are three, five and seven. No prime repeats.

marks.check: three times five and then fifteen times seven are multiplied back

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, multiply back to check. Three times five is fifteen, and fifteen times seven is one hundred and five.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>One hundred and five is the product of exactly three different primes, three times five times seven.
